description: Before 1846, patients were often awake and in extreme pain while surgeons worked. Anesthesia turned an operation into treatment instead of torture.

hero.hook: One day in 1846, in Boston, surgery stopped being a race against pain.

blocks.text: Imagine an amputation with nothing to put you to sleep. Before the middle of the 19th century, that was the norm. The patient was strapped down, the surgeon worked fast, and everyone prayed.
**Anesthesia** changed everything: it made it possible to operate without the patient feeling pain. Modern surgery could finally take its time.

blocks.caption: Without anesthesia, the surgeon had to be extremely fast

blocks.text: Surgeons were judged on their speed. Alcohol, opium, or brute force held the patient still. Many patients died of shock, of infection, or of bleeding.

blocks.caption: In Boston, a public demonstration convinced the medical world

blocks.text: On **October 16, 1846**, in Boston, the dentist **William Morton** had a patient breathe in **ether**. The surgeon **John Warren** removed a tumor from the man's neck. The patient did not scream. The room was stunned.
Warren is said to have announced: “Gentlemen, this is no humbug.” In other words, no trick. The line has stayed famous ever since.
Other products followed, such as **chloroform**, which caught on especially in Britain. Rivalries broke out over who had “invented” what. The patent hardly mattered: the idea spread around the world.
One problem remained: putting people to sleep without killing them. Doses had to be measured, breathing and the heart watched. A new specialty was born.
Today an anesthetist uses precise gases and drugs, with machines that measure everything. The whole body can be put to sleep, or only one area (local or regional anesthesia).
Since the ether demonstration of **1846**, anesthesia has transformed surgery: less pain, more time, more precision, and a level of safety that has become a science of its own.

title: The discovery of anesthesia
